claims.claim: Hook (A4): "Jupiter is the biggest planet in the solar system." A viewer who swipes at second two leaves believing only that Jupiter is the largest planet.
claims.source_checked: NASA Planetary Fact Sheet https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/ (Mass and Diameter rows)
claims.note: Jupiter has the largest mass (1898e24 kg) and diameter (142,984 km) of the eight planets. The first sentence is true by itself; nothing false is left with an early swiper.

claims.claim: "Two and a half times the mass of every other planet combined."
claims.source_checked: NASA Planetary Fact Sheet https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/ (Mass row, 10^24 kg)
claims.note: Other seven: 0.330+4.87+5.97+0.642+568+86.8+102 = 768.6; 1898/768.6 = 2.47, rounds to 2.5. Pluto/Moon correctly excluded.

claims.claim: Tag "JUPITER" / "2.5× the other planets" / "combined, by mass"
claims.source_checked: NASA Planetary Fact Sheet https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/
claims.note: Same computation as claim 2 (2.47); 'by mass' states the basis.

claims.claim: Jupiter at radius 96 with the other seven planets beneath at the same scale: Saturn 0.833, Uranus 0.363, Neptune 0.352, Earth 0.091, Venus 0.087, Mars 0.0485, Mercury 0.035 of Jupiter's radius
claims.source_checked: NASA per-planet fact sheets https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/{jupiter,saturn,uranus,neptune,earth,venus,mars,mercury}fact.html, 'Volumetric mean radius (km)'

claims.claim: "But hold Jupiter up next to the Sun, and it looks tiny." Visual: Jupiter drawn at radius 52 beside the Sun at 520
claims.source_checked: NASA Sun fact sheet https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/sunfact.html and Jupiter fact sheet .../jupiterfact.html, volumetric mean radius
claims.note: 695,700 / 69,911 = 9.95; drawn ratio 10.0 is to scale within 0.5%. 'Looks tiny' is a fair description of a body one tenth the width.

claims.claim: "It would take nearly a thousand Jupiters to fill the Sun."
claims.source_checked: NASA sunfact.html (Volume 1,412,000 x10^12 km^3) and jupiterfact.html (Volume 143,128 x10^10 km^3)
claims.note: 1,412,000e12 / 1,431.28e12 = 986.5, so 'nearly a thousand' is accurate (by volume). Mass ratio 1,988,400/1,898.13 = 1,047.6 is a different number, as SOURCES notes.

claims.claim: Tag "≈ 1,000 JUPITERS" / "to fill it, by volume" / "dots not to scale" over 1,000 small dots spread across the Sun's disc
claims.source_checked: NASA sunfact.html and jupiterfact.html volumes (as claim 6)
claims.note: ≈1,000 for 986.5 is fine; basis ('by volume') and non-scale dots are both labelled on screen (A6).

claims.claim: "Our Sun is not an average star. It is an unusually big one."
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021, A&A 650 A201, arXiv:2104.14972 LaTeX source, Table 3 (tab:numbers) and Sect. on evolved stars; Boyajian et al. 2012, ApJ 757 112, arXiv:1208.2431 LaTeX source, Table 6 (fund_params_combined.tex)
claims.note: Table 3 (Sun excluded): A 4, F 8, G 18, K 38, M 249, D 20, N/A 41. Boyajian Table 6: largest K dwarf GJ 702A 0.831 R_sun / 0.53 L_sun; Reylé text: no giants within 10 pc, only four subgiants (beta Hyi, mu Her Aa, delta Pav, delta Eri). G-or-hotter is ~8% of the neighbourhood, so 'unusually big' holds.

claims.claim: "It is bigger and brighter than over ninety percent of the stars in our part of the galaxy"
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021 arXiv:2104.14972 Table 3 and lines on subgiants and untyped objects; Boyajian et al. 2012 arXiv:1208.2431 Table 6; Giammichele, Bergeron & Dufour 2012 ApJS 199 29, arXiv:1202.5581 Table 2 (tab2.tex, parsed all 165 rows); Thévenin et al. 2005 A&A 436 253, arXiv:astro-ph/0501420 (delta Eri D/D_sun = 2.33 ± 0.03, L = 3.19 L_sun)
claims.note: Worst case: K 38 minus delta Eri (subgiant, larger and brighter) + M 249 + WD 20 = 306 of 337 typed = 90.8%; with the 41 untyped (Reylé: 36 possible M, 4 possible L, 1 possible WD, all low-mass) 347/378 = 91.8%. All M dwarfs in Boyajian Table 6 are < 0.58 R_sun and < 0.07 L_sun; WD max log L = -1.12 (WD 1620-391), within 10 pc Sirius B -1.53; Stefan-Boltzmann radii all <= 0.0216 R_sun. Both 'bigger' and 'brighter' hold; 'our part of the galaxy' matches the 10 pc scope. Could not reach CDS to confirm delta Eri is typed K in the catalogue, but the result is >90% either way.

claims.claim: Tag "THE SUN" / "bigger than 9 in 10 nearby stars"
claims.source_checked: As claim 9 (Reylé 2021 Table 3; Boyajian 2012 Table 6; Giammichele 2012 Table 2; Thévenin 2005)
claims.note: 90.8% worst case, 91.8% including untyped components: 'bigger than 9 in 10' holds; 'nearby' matches the 10 pc census.

claims.claim: "because most stars are red dwarfs"
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021 arXiv:2104.14972 Table 3 and text ('249 M stars among the 423 objects with a measured spectral type ... 58.9 ± 5.8%'; 61.3 ± 5.9% with estimated types)
claims.note: The figure is right for the 10 pc sample (249/337 typed stars = 74%; paper's own 58.9% including brown dwarfs), but the line says 'most stars', unscoped, and the only cited source is a census of the solar neighbourhood. SOURCES itself scopes claims 4 and 8 to the neighbourhood for exactly this reason. Change to 'because most of them are red dwarfs' (or 'most stars near us'), or add an A2 source for a galaxy-wide statement.

claims.claim: Red dwarfs are "small, dim, and everywhere"
claims.source_checked: Boyajian et al. 2012 arXiv:1208.2431 Table 6; Reylé et al. 2021 arXiv:2104.14972 Table 3
claims.note: M dwarfs in Table 6: 0.141 (GJ 551) to 0.577 (GJ 338A) R_sun, 0.00155 to 0.0697 L_sun. 249 of 337 typed stars within 10 pc are M (74%), which supports 'everywhere'.

claims.claim: 10x10 grid of 100 dots: 8 large bright yellow (G or hotter), 10 orange (K), 5 tiny white (white dwarfs), 77 red (M or untyped); sub "dots: star type, not size"
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021 arXiv:2104.14972 Table 3 and untyped-object paragraph
claims.note: Of 379 (337 typed + 41 untyped + Sun): G-or-hotter 31 = 8.2, K 38 = 10.0, D 20 = 5.3, M 249 + untyped 41 = 76.5 per 100; rounds to 8/10/5/77 = 100. Untyped shown as red follows Reylé's default assignment of untyped close-binary components to low-mass stars (4 possible L and 1 possible WD among them is ~1 dot, within rounding). Non-size encoding is labelled (A6).

claims.claim: "So look at the nearest star to our own. Proxima Centauri ... The closest star to the Sun"
claims.source_checked: Anglada-Escudé et al. 2016, Nature 536 437, doi:10.1038/nature19106, arXiv:1609.03449 LaTeX source (main_final.tex l.127-129)
claims.note: Text: 'At a distance of 1.295 parsecs, the red-dwarf Proxima Centauri ... is the Sun's closest stellar neighbour'. Wording 'nearest star to our own' / 'closest star to the Sun' matches.

claims.claim: "just over four light years away"
claims.source_checked: NASA Exoplanet Archive TAP, pscomppars where hostname='Proxima Cen' (sy_dist, sy_disterr1/2)

claims.claim: "you have almost certainly never seen it. It is almost always too faint for your eyes."
claims.source_checked: NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars (sy_vmag); Howard et al. 2018, ApJL 860 L30, doi:10.3847/2041-8213/aacaf3, arXiv:1804.02001 LaTeX source (abstract, l.46, l.83)
claims.note: V = 11.01, far below naked-eye limits. Howard: 'no M-dwarfs are usually visible to the naked-eye'; the March 2016 superflare (~68x) briefly made it g'=6.8, 'at the limit of visibility to trained observers at very dark sites'. That justifies both 'almost' hedges.

claims.claim: Tag "PROXIMA CENTAURI" / "≈ 1/7 the Sun's radius", drawn at 13.7 against the Sun's 96
claims.source_checked: Boyajian et al. 2012 arXiv:1208.2431 Table 6 (GJ 551 = Proxima, 0.141 ± 0.007, Demory 2009); Kervella et al. 2017, A&A 598 L7, arXiv:1611.03495 LaTeX source (l.104-107, l.316); Anglada-Escudé 2016 ('measured radius of 0.14 R_sun'); NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars st_rad = 0.141 ± 0.021 (Suárez Mascareño et al. 2025)
claims.note: 1/7 = 0.143 and 13.7/96 = 0.143, inside the interferometric 0.141 ± 0.007. Kervella's adopted 0.1542 ± 0.0045 (from the Mann et al. radius-M_Ks relation, which SOURCES calls a 'mass-radius relation') is 1/6.5; the disagreement is recorded in SOURCES per A3 and the label uses the measured value.

claims.claim: "That is what most of the stars around us look like." (the 8 bright dots fade out)
claims.source_checked: NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars st_spectype = 'M5.5 V'; Reylé et al. 2021 arXiv:2104.14972 Table 3 and text ('More than half of the M dwarfs (57.0 ± 7.3%) have spectral types M3.0 V to M5.0 V')
claims.note: Proxima is an M dwarf; M dwarfs are 249/337 = 74% of typed stars within 10 pc; 'around us' is scoped to the census.

claims.claim: "The star we call ordinary is one of the rare big ones." Sun shrinks into the grid as one of the 8; tag "THE SUN" / "one of the few"
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021 arXiv:2104.14972 Table 3 (footnote: Sun, G2 V, not included); Boyajian 2012 Table 6; Giammichele 2012 Table 2
claims.note: A 4 + F 8 + G 18 + Sun = 31 of 379 = 8%: 'rare' and 'one of the few' hold; everything outside that group (K/M dwarfs, white dwarfs, bar the subgiant delta Eri) is smaller than the Sun.

claims.claim: A1: the SOURCES block cites an A2 source for every claim
claims.source_checked: script/scale-of-the-sun.txt SOURCES entries 1-11 against the claims above
claims.note: Every spoken line and every on-screen label/visual has an entry citing NASA agency data or peer-reviewed papers with DOIs. Minor SOURCES wording nits (no script change needed): Giammichele Table 2 is 'nearby candidates' and includes a few objects beyond 20 pc; Kervella's 0.1542 comes from a radius-M_Ks relation. The scope problem in claim 11 is a wording issue in the script, not a missing citation.
